introduction-the-black-box-problem.core: Many workloads are black boxes for profiling: third-party binaries, legacy services nobody wants to touch, mixed-language fleets, and the kernel itself. SDK-based profilers need code changes, restarts and per-language setup. eBPF profilers run in the kernel and sample stacks of every process on a host from outside, giving fleet-wide, language-agnostic CPU visibility without changing or restarting anything.

first_principles.problem: A vendor-supplied binary and three legacy services in different languages consume most CPU, but none can be instrumented.
truths: Not all code can be modified.

analogy.title: A building-wide thermal camera
analogy.story: Instead of putting thermometers in every room, one camera sees where heat comes from across the whole building.
analogy.breaks: Thermal cameras show surfaces; eBPF sees stacks only if symbols are available.

check.q: What key advantage do eBPF profilers have over SDK profilers?
check.a: They profile every process on a host from the kernel with no code changes, restarts or per-language setup.

how-ebpf-actually-works-the-kernel-hook.core: eBPF lets verified programs run inside the kernel when events fire. A profiler attaches a program to a perf event, such as a CPU clock timer at 19 or 99 Hz on every core. On each tick the program captures the current kernel and user stack (bpf_get_stackid) and the PID, and increments a count in a BPF map. User space periodically reads the map, unwinds and symbolises the stacks, and ships aggregated profiles.

first_principles.problem: Engineers worry that running code in the kernel will crash production hosts.
truths: The kernel sees every context switch and tick.

analogy.title: A lighthouse keeper taking regular snapshots
analogy.story: At fixed intervals they note which ships are in the bay; counts show where traffic concentrates.
analogy.breaks: Lighthouse keepers can miss ships in fog; missing frame pointers break stack unwinding.

code.text:
bpftrace -e 'profile:hz:99 /pid > 0/ { @[ustack, comm] = count(); }' -c 'sleep 30' > stacks.txt
# feed into flamegraph.pl for a quick system-wide flamegraph

check.q: Why do eBPF profilers often sample at odd frequencies like 19 or 99 Hz?
check.a: To avoid lockstep aliasing with periodic application activity that would bias samples at round frequencies.

zero-instrumentation-no-code-changes-req.core: Zero instrumentation means deploying one privileged agent per node and getting profiles for everything, but stack quality depends on the runtime. Compiled languages need frame pointers or DWARF unwinding plus symbols; JIT and interpreted runtimes (Java, Python, Node, Ruby) need runtime-specific unwinders (perf maps, interpreter-aware unwinding) to show function names instead of interpreter internals. Modern agents increasingly handle these automatically.

first_principles.problem: An eBPF flamegraph for a Python service shows only _PyEval_EvalFrameDefault, not Python functions.
truths: Interpreters hide app frames inside their loop.
derivation: Build native code with **frame pointers** (or rely on DWARF unwinding).
Ship **debug symbols** or a symbol server.

analogy.title: Translating a recording of a foreign-language play
analogy.story: You hear the actors speaking, but without the script (symbols) you just hear sounds, not lines.
analogy.breaks: Plays have one script; each runtime needs its own unwinding approach.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Readable function names in eBPF flamegraphs.

code.text:
# Go: frame pointers on by default
# C/C++/Rust: build with frame pointers
RUSTFLAGS='-C force-frame-pointers=yes' cargo build --release
# Node.js
node --perf-basic-prof app.js
# Java: -XX:+PreserveFramePointer (+ perf map agent)

check.q: Why might an eBPF profile of a Java service show unreadable frames?
check.a: JIT-compiled code lacks symbols the kernel can resolve unless the JVM exports perf maps and preserves frame pointers.

cpu-vs-memory-profiling.core: eBPF excels at CPU profiling: timer sampling of on-CPU stacks is cheap and universal. Off-CPU profiling (time blocked on I/O, locks or sleep) uses scheduler tracepoints. Memory allocation profiling via eBPF uprobes on malloc or new is possible but costly at high allocation rates, and GC'd languages allocate inside their runtimes, so SDK profilers usually give better memory data. A common combination is eBPF for fleet CPU and SDKs for memory where needed.

first_principles.problem: A service is slow but CPU flamegraphs show little, because it spends most time waiting on locks and I/O.

analogy.title: Measuring work vs waiting
analogy.story: Watching people at desks shows working time; you also need to know how long they wait in queues.
analogy.breaks: Office queues are visible; off-CPU time needs scheduler tracing.

example.title: Off-CPU sampling

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows lock waits that CPU profiles miss.

code.text:
offcputime-bpfcc -df -p $(pgrep -n checkout) 30 > offcpu.stacks
flamegraph.pl --color=io --title='Off-CPU' < offcpu.stacks > offcpu.svg
# reveals time blocked in futex (lock contention)

example.outcome: right profile type for the question.

check.q: Why might a slow service show a small CPU flamegraph?
check.a: It's mostly waiting (off-CPU) on I/O or locks, which on-CPU sampling doesn't capture.

continuous-profiling-the-security-camera.core: Run eBPF profiling continuously, like a security camera: always recording at low overhead (around 1% CPU), with profiles stored by time and labels. When an incident or regression occurs, you rewind to that exact window and compare it against before. One-off profiling only works if you capture the moment, but intermittent and production-only issues need the history already recorded.

first_principles.problem: A 5-minute CPU spike happened at 3 a.m. and was gone before anyone could attach a profiler.

analogy.title: Security camera footage
analogy.story: You don't start recording after the burglary; you rewind the footage.
analogy.breaks: Footage is huge; profiles are compact aggregates.

example.title: Rewind
flow: Alert at 03:12: CPU spike on payments

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Root cause found after the fact.

check.q: Why is always-on profiling better than on-demand for intermittent issues?
check.a: The problem may be gone before anyone can attach a profiler; continuous profiles let you look back at that exact time.

parca-the-ebpf-specialist.core: Parca, from Polar Signals and open source, is an eBPF-native continuous profiler. Parca Agent runs as a DaemonSet, auto-discovers Kubernetes pods, samples CPU stacks at 19 Hz with DWARF-based unwinding (no frame pointers needed), and labels profiles with pod metadata. The Parca server stores profiles in a columnar format, symbolises with debuginfod, and offers flamegraphs, diffs and pprof export.

first_principles.problem: A team wants a fully open-source, eBPF-first profiler that handles binaries without frame pointers.
truths: DWARF info can unwind without frame pointers.

analogy.title: A specialist sports photographer
analogy.story: Focused on one technique (eBPF), with special lenses (DWARF unwinding) to capture shots others can't.
analogy.breaks: Photographers choose shots; Parca samples everything.

code.text:
helm repo add parca https://parca-dev.github.io/helm-charts
helm install parca parca/parca -n parca --create-namespace
kubectl -n parca port-forward svc/parca 7070
# query: parca_agent:samples:count:cpu:nanoseconds:delta{namespace="shop"}

check.q: What does DWARF-based unwinding let Parca do?
check.a: Reconstruct stacks for binaries compiled without frame pointers, using debug/unwind information.

pyroscope-the-polyglot-profiler.core: Grafana Pyroscope supports both worlds: language SDKs (Go, Java, Python, Ruby, .NET, Node, Rust) for rich CPU, allocation, lock and wall profiles with custom labels, and eBPF collection through Grafana Alloy for zero-instrumentation coverage. It integrates tightly with Grafana (traces-to-profiles, dashboards) and stores profiles in object storage, so teams pick per service.

first_principles.problem: A polyglot company wants deep memory profiles for key Go and Java services and basic CPU coverage for everything else.

analogy.title: A clinic with both GPs and specialists
analogy.story: Everyone gets a general check-up (eBPF); key patients see specialists (SDKs).
analogy.breaks: Clinics refer patients; you choose instrumentation per service.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: All pods CPU-profiled; SDK services add memory.

check.q: Why combine SDK and eBPF profiling in one platform?
check.a: eBPF gives cheap universal CPU coverage, while SDKs add memory, lock profiles and labels where depth matters.

the-visualization-reading-flamegraphs.core: Reading eBPF flamegraphs adds a few twists. Kernel frames appear at the bottom (syscalls, network stack, page faults), and wide kernel towers mean heavy syscalls or I/O. Process and container labels let you filter. Unsymbolised frames show as addresses, which points to missing symbols. Use diff views (red grew, blue shrank) between versions, and sandwich views to see all callers and callees of a function.

first_principles.problem: A flamegraph shows a wide tower of 'tcp_sendmsg' and hex addresses, and the team can't interpret it.
truths: Kernel and user frames appear together.

analogy.title: Reading a building's floor plan including the basement
analogy.story: The basement (kernel) holds plumbing that every floor uses; a busy pipe shows up under many rooms.
analogy.breaks: Floor plans are fixed; profiles change with load.

check.q: What does a wide kernel syscall tower under an app function suggest?
check.a: The app is making many or expensive syscalls (e.g., small unbuffered writes), so batching or buffering may help.
